questions.question: \(\mathbf{x} = [x_1 \;\; x_2 \;\; \dots \;\; x_n]^{\top}\) is an \(n\)-tuple nonzero vector. The \(n \times n\) matrix \(\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{x}\mathbf{x}^{\top}\)
questions.explanation:
Let \(X\) be a non-zero column vector of dimensions \(n \times 1\). The matrix \(V\) is defined as the outer product of the vector \(X\) with its own transpose \(X^{\top}\): \[V = \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \\ \vdots \\ \vdots \\ x_n \end{bmatrix}_{n \times 1} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 & x_2 & \dots & \dots & x_n \end{bmatrix}_{1 \times n} = XX^{\top}\]
Method 1
By performing standard matrix multiplication row-by-row, the resulting square matrix \(V\) of size \(n \times n\) is explicitly structured as: \[V = \begin{bmatrix} x_1x_1 & x_1x_2 & \dots & x_1x_n \\ x_2x_1 & x_2x_2 & \dots & x_2x_n \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ x_nx_1 & x_nx_2 & \dots & x_nx_n \end{bmatrix}_{n \times n}\] Let us analyze the rows of matrix \(V\): \[\begin{aligned} R_1 &= x_1 \begin{bmatrix} x_1 & x_2 & \dots & x_n \end{bmatrix} \\ R_2 &= x_2 \begin{bmatrix} x_1 & x_2 & \dots & x_n \end{bmatrix} = \frac{x_2}{x_1} R_1 \quad (\text{for } x_1 \neq 0) \\ &\vdots \\ R_n &= x_n \begin{bmatrix} x_1 & x_2 & \dots & x_n \end{bmatrix} = \frac{x_n}{x_1} R_1 \quad (\text{for } x_1 \neq 0) \end{aligned}\] Since every row \(R_i\) is a scalar multiple of the first row \(R_1\), all rows are linearly dependent on a single basis row. Performing elementary row operations can reduce all rows except one to zero. Therefore, the number of linearly independent rows is exactly \(1\), which means: \[\rho(V) = 1\]
Method 2
We can alternatively find the rank of matrix \(V\) using properties of matrix rank inequalities. For any product of two matrices \(A\) and \(B\), the rank of the product is bounded by: \[\rho(AB) \le \min\left(\rho(A), \rho(B)\right)\] Substituting \(A = X_{n \times 1}\) and \(B = X^{\top}_{1 \times n}\) into the inequality: \[\rho(V) = \rho\left(XX^{\top}\right) \le \min\left(\rho(X_{n \times 1}), \rho(X^{\top}_{1 \times n})\right)\] Since \(X\) is a non-zero column vector and \(X^{\top}\) is a non-zero row vector, both contain exactly one linearly independent vector asset: \[\rho(X_{n \times 1}) = 1 \quad \text{and} \quad \rho(X^{\top}_{1 \times n}) = 1\] Thus: \[\rho(V) \le \min(1, 1) \implies \rho(V) \le 1\] Because \(X\) is a non-zero vector, \(V\) is a non-zero matrix, which ensures \(\rho(V) \ge 1\). Combining these upper and lower limits gives: \[\rho(V) = 1\]
\[\boxed{\text{(B) has rank $1$}}\]
Key points
  • Rank of an Outer Product: The outer product of any two non-zero column vectors \(u\) and \(v\) always structures a rank-one matrix: \(\rho(uv^{\top}) = 1\).
  • Linear Dependence in Outer Products: In an outer product matrix \(V = uv^{\top}\), every column is a scalar multiple of \(u\), and every row is a scalar multiple of \(v^{\top}\).
Mistakes to avoid
  • Outer Product vs. Inner Product: Do not confuse the outer product matrix \(XX^{\top}\) (which is an \(n \times n\) matrix of rank 1) with the inner product scalar \(X^{\top}X\) (which is a \(1 \times 1\) scalar value representing the squared Euclidean norm \(\|X\|^2\)).
  • Vector Dimension Formats: Ensure that the matrix dimension layouts like \(X_{n \times 1}\) and \(X^{\top}_{1 \times n}\) are placed in math mode with proper formatting instead of written as unformatted text.

questions.question: Let \(x\) and \(y\) be two vectors in a \(3\) dimensional space and \(\langle x,y \rangle\) denote their dot product. Then the determinant \[\det \begin{bmatrix} \langle x,x \rangle & \langle x,y \rangle \\ \langle y,x \rangle & \langle y,y \rangle \end{bmatrix}\]
options: is zero when \(x\) and \(y\) are linearly independent
is positive when \(x\) and \(y\) are linearly independent
is non-zero for all non-zero \(x\) and \(y\)
is zero only when either \(x\) or \(y\) is zero
questions.explanation: Let \(x\) and \(y\) be two real vectors in a \(3\)-dimensional Euclidean space, and let \(\langle x,y \rangle\) denote their standard inner product (dot product), which can also be written as \(x \cdot y\). \[G = \det \begin{bmatrix} \langle x,x \rangle & \langle x,y \rangle \\ \langle y,x \rangle & \langle y,y \rangle \end{bmatrix}\] \[G = \det \begin{bmatrix} \|x\|^2 & x \cdot y \\ x \cdot y & \|y\|^2 \end{bmatrix}\] \[G = \|x\|^2 \|y\|^2 - (x \cdot y)^2 \qquad \text{--- (1)}\] \[|x \cdot y| \le \|x\| \|y\|\] \[(x \cdot y)^2 \le \|x\|^2 \|y\|^2 \implies \|x\|^2 \|y\|^2 - (x \cdot y)^2 \ge 0\] The equality condition for Cauchy-Schwarz states that \((x \cdot y)^2 = \|x\|^2 \|y\|^2\) if and only if the vectors \(x\) and \(y\) are linearly dependent. Therefore, if \(x\) and \(y\) are **linearly independent**, the strict inequality holds: \[(x \cdot y)^2 < \|x\|^2 \|y\|^2 \implies \|x\|^2 \|y\|^2 - (x \cdot y)^2 > 0\] Thus, the determinant is strictly positive when \(x\) and \(y\) are linearly independent. \[\boxed{\text{(B) is positive when $x$ and $y$ are linearly independent}}\]

questions.question: The linear operation \(L(\mathbf{x})\) is defined by the cross product \(L(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{x}\), where \(\mathbf{b} = [0 \;\; 1 \;\; 0]^{\top}\) and \(\mathbf{x} = [x_1 \;\; x_2 \;\; x_3]^{\top}\) are three dimensional vectors. The \(3 \times 3\) matrix \(M\) of this operation satisfies \[L(\mathbf{x}) = M \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}\] Then the eigenvalues of \(M\) are
questions.explanation:
Given the linear operation \(L(\mathbf{x})\) defined by a vector cross product: \[L(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{x}\] where \(\mathbf{b} = [0 \;\; 1 \;\; 0]^{\top}\) and \(\mathbf{x} = [x_1 \;\; x_2 \;\; x_3]^{\top}\). We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix \(M\) that satisfies: \[L(\mathbf{x}) = M \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}\] Let us compute the cross product \(\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{x}\) explicitly using the standard determinant definition with unit vectors \(\hat{i}\), \(\hat{j}\), and \(\hat{k}\): \[\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{x} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ x_1 & x_2 & x_3 \end{vmatrix}\] \[\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{x} = \hat{i}(1 \cdot x_3 - 0 \cdot x_2) - \hat{j}(0 \cdot x_3 - 0 \cdot x_1) + \hat{k}(0 \cdot x_2 - 1 \cdot x_1)\] \[\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{x} = x_3\hat{i} + 0\hat{j} - x_1\hat{k}\] \[L(\mathbf{x}) = \begin{bmatrix} x_3 \\ 0 \\ -x_1 \end{bmatrix}\] \[\begin{bmatrix} x_3 \\ 0 \\ -x_1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \cdot x_1 + 0 \cdot x_2 + 1 \cdot x_3 \\ 0 \cdot x_1 + 0 \cdot x_2 + 0 \cdot x_3 \\ -1 \cdot x_1 + 0 \cdot x_2 + 0 \cdot x_3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}\] Thus, the matrix \(M\) is: \[M = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\] Now, we determine the eigenvalues (\(\lambda\)) of matrix \(M\) using the characteristic equation \(|M - \lambda I| = 0\): \[\begin{vmatrix} -\lambda & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & -\lambda & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & -\lambda \end{vmatrix} = 0\] \[(-\lambda) \begin{vmatrix} -\lambda & 1 \\ -1 & -\lambda \end{vmatrix} = 0\] \[(-\lambda) \left[(-\lambda)(-\lambda) - (1)(-1)\right] = 0\] \[-\lambda \left(\lambda^2 + 1\right) = 0\]
  • \(-\lambda = 0 \implies \lambda = 0\)
  • \(\lambda^2 + 1 = 0 \implies \lambda^2 = -1 \implies \lambda = \pm i\)
Hence, the eigenvalues of \(M\) are \(i, -i, 0\). \[\boxed{\text{(D) $i, -i, 0$}}\]

Answer Questions Q1.07.4 and Q1.07.5 using the following data. Cayley-Hamilton Theorem states that a square matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation. Consider a matrix: \[A = \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\]

\(A\) satisfies the relation
questions.explanation: The characteristic equation of a square matrix \(A\) is determined by finding the roots of its characteristic polynomial: \[|A - \lambda I| = 0\] Given the characteristic determinant layout for the \(2 \times 2\) matrix: \[\begin{vmatrix} -3 - \lambda & 2 \\ -1 & 0 - \lambda \end{vmatrix} = 0\] Expanding the \(2 \times 2\) determinant explicitly: \[(-3 - \lambda)(0 - \lambda) - (2)(-1) = 0\] \[\lambda(3 + \lambda) + 2 = 0\] \[\lambda^2 + 3\lambda + 2 = 0\] \[A^2 + 3A + 2I = O\] \[A^2 + 2A + A + 2I = O\] \[A(A + 2I) + I(A + 2I) = O\] \[(A + I)(A + 2I) = O\] \[\boxed{\text{(C) $(A + I)(A + 2I) = 0$}}\]

questions.question:
Answer Questions Q1.07.4 and Q1.07.5 using the following data. Cayley-Hamilton Theorem states that a square matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation. Consider a matrix: \[A = \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\]

\(A^9\) equals
questions.explanation:
The characteristic equation of a square matrix \(A\) is given by: \[|A - \lambda I| = 0\] \[\begin{vmatrix} -3 - \lambda & 2 \\ -1 & 0 - \lambda \end{vmatrix} = 0\] \[(-3 - \lambda)(0 - \lambda) - (2)(-1) = 0\] \[\lambda^2 - (-3)\lambda + 2 = 0\] \[\lambda^2 + 3\lambda + 2 = 0\]
Method 1
According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem: \[A^2 + 3A + 2I = O\] \[\implies A^2 = -3A - 2I \qquad \text{--- (1)}\] \[A^3 = A \cdot A^2 = A(-3A - 2I) = -3A^2 - 2A\] \[A^3 = -3(-3A - 2I) - 2A = 9A + 6I - 2A\] \[\implies A^3 = 7A + 6I \qquad \text{--- (2)}\] \[A^4 = A \cdot A^3 = A(7A + 6I) = 7A^2 + 6A\] \[A^4 = 7(-3A - 2I) + 6A = -21A - 14I + 6A\] \[\implies A^4 = -15A - 14I \qquad \text{--- (3)}\] \[A^5 = A \cdot A^4 = A(-15A - 14I) = -15A^2 - 14A\] \[A^5 = -15(-3A - 2I) - 14A = 45A + 30I - 14A\] \[\implies A^5 = 31A + 30I \qquad \text{--- (4)}\] By observing the structural coefficient pattern generated across equations (1), (2), (3), and (4): \[\begin{aligned} A^1 &= 1A + 0I \\ A^2 &= -3A - 2I \\ A^3 &= 7A + 6I \\ A^4 &= -15A - 14I \\ A^5 &= 31A + 30I \end{aligned}\] Let us look at the coefficients of \(A\) and \(I\) for any power \(n\). Let \(A^n = c_n A + d_n I\). The sequence of the \(A\) coefficients (\(1, -3, 7, -15, 31, \dots\)) satisfies the clear pattern: \[c_n = (-1)^{n-1}(2^n - 1)\] For \(n = 9\): \[c_9 = (-1)^{8}(2^9 - 1) = 1 \cdot (512 - 1) = 511\] The sequence of the \(I\) coefficients (\(0, -2, 6, -14, 30, \dots\)) satisfies the pattern: \[d_n = c_n - 1 \quad \text{(for odd $n$)} \quad \text{or} \quad d_n = c_n + 1 \quad \text{(for even $n$)}\] More universally, \(d_n = (-1)^{n-1}(2^n - 1) - (-1)^{n-1} = (-1)^{n-1}(2^n - 2)\). For \(n = 9\): \[d_9 = (-1)^{8}(2^9 - 2) = 1 \cdot (512 - 2) = 510\] Thus, assembling the expression for \(A^9\): \[A^9 = 511A + 510I\]
Method 2
We can solve this problem much faster using a remainder polynomial evaluation technique. Let us find the remainder when \(\lambda^9\) is divided by the characteristic polynomial \(p(\lambda) = \lambda^2 + 3\lambda + 2\). Since the divisor is a second-degree polynomial, the remainder must be a linear polynomial of the form \(a\lambda + b\): \[\lambda^9 = q(\lambda)(\lambda^2 + 3\lambda + 2) + (a\lambda + b)\] Factoring the characteristic polynomial: \[\lambda^2 + 3\lambda + 2 = (\lambda + 1)(\lambda + 2)\] Thus, the roots (eigenvalues) are \(\lambda = -1\) and \(\lambda = -2\). Substituting these roots into the identity equation:
  • For \(\lambda = -1\): \[(-1)^9 = q(-1)(0) + a(-1) + b \implies -a + b = -1 \qquad \text{--- (5)}\]
  • For \(\lambda = -2\): \[(-2)^9 = q(-2)(0) + a(-2) + b \implies -2a + b = -512 \qquad \text{--- (6)}\]
Subtracting equation (6) from equation (5): \[(-a + b) - (-2a + b) = -1 - (-512)\] \[a = 511\] Substituting \(a = 511\) back into equation (5): \[-511 + b = -1 \implies b = 510\] Therefore, the scalar remainder polynomial is \(511\lambda + 510\). By applying the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we can substitute the matrix configurations directly into this remainder expression: \[A^9 = 511A + 510I\]
\[\boxed{\text{(A) $511 \, A + 510 \, I$}}\]
Key points
  • Cayley-Hamilton Polynomial Division Property: Any high-order matrix power \(A^n\) can be simplified to a lower-degree matrix polynomial matching the exact remainder obtained by dividing \(\lambda^n\) by the characteristic polynomial of \(A\).
  • Commutative Reduction: Substituting matrix variables into verified scalar remainder identities is valid because all constituent components (\(A^n\), \(A\), and \(I\)) commute perfectly with each other.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Remainder Bounds: When setting up a remainder function for polynomial long division, always make sure its degree is strictly less than the degree of the characteristic polynomial (\(\text{deg}(r) < \text{deg}(p)\)). For a \(2 \times 2\) matrix, the remainder is always at most linear (\(aA + bI\)).

questions.question: Consider the function \(f(x) = (x^2 - 4)^2\) where \(x\) is a real number. Then the function has
questions.explanation:
Given the real-valued function: \[f(x) = (x^2 - 4)^2\] To find the critical points, we differentiate \(f(x)\) with respect to \(x\) using the chain rule: \[f'(x) = 2(x^2 - 4) \cdot \frac{d}{dx}(x^2 - 4)\] \[f'(x) = 2(x^2 - 4)(2x) = 4x(x^2 - 4)\] Setting the first derivative to zero to identify the stationary points: \[4x(x^2 - 4) = 0\] \[4x(x - 2)(x + 2) = 0 \implies x = 0, \; x = 2, \; x = -2\] To determine the nature of these stationary points, we find the second derivative \(f''(x)\): \[f'(x) = 4x^3 - 16x\] \[f''(x) = \frac{d}{dx}(4x^3 - 16x) = 12x^2 - 16\] Now, we evaluate the second derivative at each stationary point:
  • At \(x = 0\):
    \[f''(0) = 12(0)^2 - 16 = -16 < 0\] Since \(f''(0) < 0\), \(x = 0\) is a point of local maximum.
  • At \(x = 2\):
    \[f''(2) = 12(2)^2 - 16 = 12(4) - 16 = 48 - 16 = 32 > 0\] Since \(f''(2) > 0\), \(x = 2\) is a point of local minimum.
  • At \(x = -2\):
    \[f''(-2) = 12(-2)^2 - 16 = 12(4) - 16 = 48 - 16 = 32 > 0\] Since \(f''(-2) > 0\), \(x = -2\) is a point of local minimum.
Thus, the function possesses exactly two distinct minima (occurring at \(x = \pm 2\)). \[\boxed{\text{(b) Only two minima}}\]

questions.question: The integral \(\dfrac{1}{2\pi} \int_{0}^{2\pi} \sin (t - \tau) \cos \tau \, d\tau\) equals
questions.explanation:
We need to evaluate the definite integral: \[I = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{0}^{2\pi} \sin(t - \tau) \cos\tau \, d\tau\] Using the trigonometric product-to-sum identity: \[2\sin A \cos B = \sin(A + B) + \sin(A - B)\] Here, setting \(A = t - \tau\) and \(B = \tau\): \[\sin(t - \tau) \cos\tau = \frac{1}{2} \Big[ \sin((t - \tau) + \tau) + \sin((t - \tau) - \tau) \Big]\] \[\sin(t - \tau) \cos\tau = \frac{1}{2} \Big[ \sin t + \sin(t - 2\tau) \Big]\] Substituting this back into the integral: \[I = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{0}^{2\pi} \frac{1}{2} \Big[ \sin t + \sin(t - 2\tau) \Big] \, d\tau\] \[I = \frac{1}{4\pi} \left[ \int_{0}^{2\pi} \sin t \, d\tau + \int_{0}^{2\pi} \sin(t - 2\tau) \, d\tau \right]\] Integrating each component with respect to \(\tau\) (treating \(t\) as a constant):
  • First Integral:
    \[\int_{0}^{2\pi} \sin t \, d\tau = \sin t \cdot \Big[ \tau \Big]_{0}^{2\pi} = 2\pi \sin t\]
  • Second Integral:
    \[\int_{0}^{2\pi} \sin(t - 2\tau) \, d\tau = \left[ \frac{-\cos(t - 2\tau)}{-2} \right]_{0}^{2\pi} = \frac{1}{2} \Big[ \cos(t - 2\tau) \Big]_{0}^{2\pi}\] Evaluating at the boundaries: \[\frac{1}{2} \Big[ \cos(t - 4\pi) - \cos(t - 0) \Big]\] Since cosine is periodic with a period of \(2\pi\), \(\cos(t - 4\pi) = \cos t\): \[\frac{1}{2} \Big[ \cos t - \cos t \Big] = 0\]
Combining both components together: \[I = \frac{1}{4\pi} \Big[ 2\pi \sin t + 0 \Big] = \frac{2\pi \sin t}{4\pi} = \frac{1}{2}\sin t\] \[\boxed{\text{(d) } \frac{1}{2} \sin t}\]

questions.question: The value of \(\oint_{C} \dfrac{dz}{(1+z^2)}\) where \(C\) is the contour \(\left| z - i/2 \right| = 1\) is
questions.explanation:
Given integral is: \[I = \oint_{C} \frac{dz}{1+z^2} = \oint_{C} \frac{dz}{(z+i)(z-i)}\] The integrand \(f(z) = \frac{1}{1+z^2}\) has simple poles at: \[z = -i\] \[z = i\] The given contour \(C\) is a circle described by: \[\left| z - \frac{i}{2} \right| = 1\] Checking the position of the poles with respect to the contour \(C\):
  • For \(z = i\): \(\left| i - \frac{i}{2} \right| = \left| \frac{i}{2} \right| = \frac{1}{2} < 1\) (Lies inside \(C\))
  • For \(z = -i\): \(\left| -i - \frac{i}{2} \right| = \left| -\frac{3i}{2} \right| = \frac{3}{2} > 1\) (Lies outside \(C\))
Therefore, \(z = i\) will lie inside contour \(C\). [figure unavailable] By Cauchy's Residue Theorem: \[\oint_{C} \frac{dz}{1+z^2} = 2\pi i \left[ \text{Res } f(z) \text{ at } z=i \right]\] \[\oint_{C} \frac{dz}{1+z^2} = 2\pi i \left\{ \frac{1}{i+i} \right\} = 2\pi i \left\{ \frac{1}{2i} \right\} = \pi\] \[\boxed{B. \pi}\]

questions.question: In the circuit shown in figure switch \(\text{SW}_1\) is initially CLOSED and \(\text{SW}_2\) is OPEN. The inductor L carries a current of \(10\text{A}\) and the capacitor is charged to \(10\text{ V}\) with polarities as indicated. \(\text{SW}_2\), is initially CLOSED at \(t = 0^{-}\) and \(\text{SW}_1\), is OPENED at \(t = 0\). The current through \(\text{C}\) and the voltage across \(\text{L}\) at \(t = 0^{+}\) is
questions.explanation: Before switching, \[i_L(0^-)=10~\text{A}, \qquad v_C(0^-)=10~\text{V}\] Since inductor current and capacitor voltage cannot change instantaneously, \[i_L(0^+)=i_L(0^-)=10~\text{A}\] \[v_C(0^+)=v_C(0^-)=10~\text{V}\] Thus, at \(t=0^+\), the inductor can be represented by a \(10~\text{A}\) current source. Circuit at \(t=0^+\) Applying KCL at node \(V_L\), \[\frac{V_L}{10} + \frac{V_L-10}{10} - 10 = 0\] Multiplying throughout by \(10\), \[V_L+V_L-10-100=0\] \[2V_L=110 \ \Rightarrow \ V_L=55~\text{V}\] Hence, \[v_L(0^+)=55~\text{V}\] Now, \[i_C(0^+) = \frac{V_L-10}{10}\] \[i_C(0^+) = \frac{55-10}{10} = \frac{45}{10} = 4.5~\text{A}\] Hence, \[\boxed{\textbf{D. }\;4.5~\text{A},\;55~\text{V}}\]

questions.question: The R-L-C series circuit shown is supplied from a variable frequency voltage source. The admittance-locus of the R-L-C network at terminals ABfor increasing frequency \(\omega\) is
questions.explanation:
The complex admittance \(Y\) of a series \(RLC\) circuit is defined as the reciprocal of its total impedance \(Z\): \[Y = \frac{1}{R + j\left(\omega L - \dfrac{1}{\omega C}\right)}\] To separate the real and imaginary components, multiply the numerator and denominator by the complex conjugate of the impedance: \[Y = \frac{R - j\left(\omega L - \dfrac{1}{\omega C}\right)}{R^{2} + \left(\omega L - \dfrac{1}{\omega C}\right)^{2}}\] Extracting the real part of the admittance \(\text{Re}(Y)\), which represents the conductance \(G\): \[\text{Re}(Y) = \frac{R}{R^{2} + \left(\omega L - \dfrac{1}{\omega C}\right)^{2}}\] Since \(R\) and the squared term in the denominator are always non-negative, the real part \(\text{Re}(Y)\) will always be positive. At the resonant frequency \(\omega_{0} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}\), the reactive terms cancel each other out (\(\omega_{0} L = \frac{1}{\omega_{0} C}\)), making the denominator minimum and driving \(\text{Re}(Y)\) to its maximum value: \[\text{Re}(Y)_{max} = \frac{1}{R}\] Now, extracting the imaginary part of the admittance \(\text{Im}(Y)\), which represents the susceptance \(B\): \[\text{Im}(Y) = \frac{\dfrac{1}{\omega C} - \omega L}{R^{2} + \left(\omega L - \dfrac{1}{\omega C}\right)^{2}}\] Let us evaluate the behavior of \(\text{Im}(Y)\) across different frequency ranges relative to the resonant frequency \(\omega_{0}\):
  • At resonance (\(\omega = \omega_{0}\)): Since \(\frac{1}{\omega_{0} C} = \omega_{0} L\), the numerator becomes zero, yielding \(\text{Im}(Y) = 0\).
  • Below resonance (\(0 < \omega < \omega_{0}\)): The capacitive reactance dominates over the inductive reactance (\(\frac{1}{\omega C} > \omega L\)), making the numerator positive. Hence, \(\text{Im}(Y) > 0\) (capacitive susceptance).
  • Above resonance (\(\omega_{0} < \omega < \infty\)): The inductive reactance dominates (\(\frac{1}{\omega C} < \omega L\)), making the numerator negative. Hence, \(\text{Im}(Y) < 0\) (inductive susceptance).
  • At extreme limits (\(\omega \to 0\) and \(\omega \to \infty\)): The admittance magnitudes drop to zero, converging at the origin \((0,0)\).
Plotting \(\text{Re}(Y)\) on the real axis and \(\text{Im}(Y)\) on the imaginary axis as frequency \(\omega\) varies from \(0\) to \(\infty\) forms a circular trajectory located entirely in the right-half plane. The locus is a circle with a diameter of \(\frac{1}{R}\) passing through the origin, centered on the real axis at \(\left(\frac{1}{2R}, 0\right)\).
Key points
  • At resonance, the network is purely resistive; the admittance is real and reaches its absolute peak value of \(\frac{1}{R}\).

Let the reactance of the capacitor be \(X_{C}\). The circuit current phasor \(I\) can be expressed by analyzing the parallel configuration or loop equations matching the system: \[I = \frac{V\angle 0^\circ + V\angle 0^\circ}{R + jX_{C}}\] Simplifying the numerator for identical in-phase sources yields: \[I = \frac{2V}{R - jX_{C}}\] Applying Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL) to determine the terminal voltage \(V_{YX}\): \[V_{YX} - V\angle 0^\circ + IR = 0\] Rearranging the expression to solve for \(V_{YX}\): \[V_{YX} = V - IR\] Substituting the expression for current \(I\) into the KVL equation: \[V_{YX} = V - \frac{2V}{R - jX_{C}} \times R\] Factoring out the voltage term \(V\) and finding a common denominator simplifies the complex expression to: \[V_{YX} = -V \left( \frac{R + jX_{C}}{R - jX_{C}} \right)\] Let us evaluate the boundary behaviors of the terminal voltage \(V_{YX}\) at extreme structural values of the variable resistor \(R\):
  • When \(R = 0\): \[V_{YX} = -V \left( \frac{0 + jX_{C}}{0 - jX_{C}} \right) = -V(-1) = V\]
  • When \(R = \infty\): \[V_{YX} = -V\]
As the resistance \(R\) varies continuously from \(0\) to \(\infty\), the magnitude of the rational multiplier remains constant at unity, i.e., \(\left| \frac{R + jX_{C}}{R - jX_{C}} \right| = 1\), while its phase shifts. questions.question: Let a signal \(a_1\sin(\omega_1 t+\phi_1)\) be applied to a stable linear time-invariant system. Let the corresponding steady state output be represented as \(a_2F(\omega_2 t+\phi_2)\). Then which of the following statements is true?
options: \(F\) is not necessarily a ``sine'' or ``cosine'' function but must be periodic with \(\omega_1=\omega_2\).
\(F\) must be a ``sine'' or ``cosine'' function with \(a_1=a_2\).
\(F\) must be a ``sine'' function with \(\omega_1=\omega_2\) and \(\phi_1=\phi_2\).
\(F\) must be a ``sine'' or ``cosine'' function with \(\omega_1=\omega_2\).
questions.explanation:
A stable LTI system is excited by the sinusoidal input \[x(t)=a_{1}\sin(\omega_{1}t+\phi_{1}).\] For a stable LTI system, a sinusoidal input produces a sinusoidal steady-state output of the same frequency. Only the amplitude and phase are modified by the system. Hence, \[y_{ss}(t)=a_{2}\sin(\omega_{1}t+\phi_{2}),\] or equivalently, \[y_{ss}(t)=a_{2}\cos(\omega_{1}t+\phi),\] since sine and cosine differ only by a phase shift. Therefore, \[\omega_{2}=\omega_{1},\] and \(F(\cdot)\) must be either a sine or a cosine function. Checking the options:
  • A. False: \(F\) cannot be an arbitrary periodic function.
  • B. False: The amplitude generally changes, so \(a_{1}\neq a_{2}\) in general.
  • C. False: The phase need not remain unchanged.
  • D. True: \(F\) must be a sine or cosine function with \(\omega_{1}=\omega_{2}\).
\[\boxed{\text{(d) }F\text{ must be a ``sine'' or ``cosine'' function with }\omega_{1}=\omega_{2}.}\]

r(t-2)=r\!\left(t-2\right),\] we obtain \[u(t+1)*r(t-2)

u(t)*r(t)

questions.explanation:
The given FIR filter is \[G(z)=\alpha z^{-1}+\beta z^{-3}.\] Its impulse response is \[h[n]=\{0,\alpha,0,\beta\}.\] For an FIR filter to have linear phase, the impulse response must be symmetric or anti-symmetric. Symmetric condition: \[h[1]=h[3] \quad\Rightarrow\quad \alpha=\beta.\] Anti-symmetric condition: \[h[1]=-h[3] \quad\Rightarrow\quad \alpha=-\beta.\] Since the filter is specified to be a low-pass filter, the DC gain must be non-zero. Now, \[G(e^{j0})=\alpha+\beta.\] If \[\alpha=-\beta,\] then \[G(e^{j0})=0,\] which cannot represent a low-pass filter. Hence, the valid condition is \[\alpha=\beta.\] \[\boxed{\text{(a) }\alpha=\beta.}\]
Key points
  • Linear-phase FIR filters require symmetric or anti-symmetric impulse responses.
  • Low-pass FIR filters require a symmetric impulse response.
  • Anti-symmetric FIR filters have zero DC gain.

questions.question: The circuit shown in the figure is
options: a voltage source with voltage \(\dfrac{rV}{R_1 \parallel R_2}\)
a voltage source with voltage \(\dfrac{r \parallel R_2}{R_1}V\)
a current source with current \(\dfrac{r \parallel R_2}{R_1 + R_2} \cdot \dfrac{V}{r}\)
a current source with current \(\dfrac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2} \cdot \dfrac{V}{r}\)
questions.explanation:
The voltage at the non-inverting terminal (\(V_+\)) of the op-amp is determined by the voltage divider formed by \(R_1\) and \(R_2\): \[V_+ = V \left( \frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2} \right)\] Due to virtual short concept under negative feedback: \[V_- = V_+ = V \left( \frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2} \right)\] The current through the resistor \(r\) (which is equal to the load current \(I_{\text{L}}\) since no current enters the op-amp inverting terminal) is given by: \[I_{\text{L}} = \frac{V_-}{r} = \frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2} \cdot \frac{V}{r}\] Since \(I_{\text{L}}\) is independent of the load resistance, the circuit acts as a current source. \[\boxed{\text{(D) a current source with current $\dfrac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2} \cdot \dfrac{V}{r}$}}\]
Key points
Op-Amp Voltage-Controlled Current Source: Using negative feedback, an op-amp maintains a fixed voltage across a current-sensing resistor \(r\), forcing a constant load current independent of load impedance.

questions.question: The switch S in the circuit of the figure is initially closed. It is opened at time \(t = 0\). You may neglect the Zener diode forward voltage drops. What is the behaviour of \(V_{\text{OUT}}\) for \(t > 0\)?
options: It makes a transition from \(-5\text{ V}\) to \(+5\text{ V}\) at \(t = 12.98\ \mu\text{s}\)
It makes a transition from \(-5\text{ V}\) to \(+5\text{ V}\) at \(t = 2.57\ \mu\text{s}\)
It makes a transition from \(+5\text{ V}\) to \(-5\text{ V}\) at \(t = 12.98\ \mu\text{s}\)
It makes a transition from \(+5\text{ V}\) to \(-5\text{ V}\) at \(t = 2.57\ \mu\text{s}\)
questions.explanation:
At \(t = 0^-\), switch S is closed, shorting the capacitor to \(-10\,\text{V}\), so \(V_-(0^-) = -10\,\text{V}\). Since \(V_-(0^+) = -10\,\text{V} < V_+\), the initial output is clamped by the back-to-back Zener diodes: \[V_{\text{OUT}}(0^+) = +5\,\text{V}\] The non-inverting terminal voltage \(V_+\) is: \[V_+ = V_{\text{OUT}} \left( \frac{100\,\text{k}\Omega}{100\,\text{k}\Omega + 10\,\text{k}\Omega} \right) = \frac{50}{11}\,\text{V} \approx 4.545\,\text{V}\] Time constant of the charging circuit: \[\tau = R C = (1\,\text{k}\Omega)(0.01\,\mu\text{F}) = 10\,\mu\text{s}\] For \(t > 0\), the capacitor charges towards \(+10\,\text{V}\): \[V_-(t) = V_f + (V_i - V_f)e^{-t/\tau}\] \[= 10 + (-10 - 10)e^{-t/\tau}\] \[V_-(t) = 10 - 20 e^{-10^5 t}\] The output \(V_{\text{OUT}}\) switches from \(+5\,\text{V}\) to \(-5\,\text{V}\) when \(V_-(t)\) reaches \(V_+\): \[\frac{50}{11} = 10 - 20 e^{-10^5 t}\] \[e^{10^5 t} = \frac{220}{60} \implies 10^5 t = \ln\left(\frac{11}{3}\right) \approx 1.2993\] \[t = 12.98\,\mu\text{s}\] Thus, \(V_{\text{OUT}}\) transitions from \(+5\,\text{V}\) to \(-5\,\text{V}\) at \(t = 12.98\,\mu\text{s}\). \[\boxed{\text{(C)}}\]
Key points
  • Comparator Thresholding: The transition occurs when the charging capacitor voltage at the inverting terminal crosses the non-inverting reference voltage \(V_+\).
  • Zener Clamping: Back-to-back Zener diodes limit the output voltage swing to \(\pm V_Z\).

questions.question: The common emitter forward current gain of the transistor is \(\beta_F = 100\). The transistor is operating in
questions.explanation:
Given:
  • (i) \(p\)-\(n\)-\(p\) transistor
  • (ii) \(\beta_F = 100\)
Since, emitter junction is in forward bias region due to \(10\,\text{V}\) voltage source, hence BJT will be either in active region or in saturation region.
Method 1
Assuming transistor is in active region, \[V_{EB(\text{active})} = 0.7\,\text{V}\] Applying KVL in loop (1), \[-10 + (1+\beta)I_B \times 1 + V_{EB(\text{active})} + 270 \times I_B = 0\] \[-10 + 371 I_B + 0.7 = 0\] \[I_B = 0.025\,\text{mA}\] Collector current is given by, \[I_C = \beta I_B = 100 \times 0.025 = 2.5\,\text{mA}\] Applying KVL in loop (2), \[-I_B \times 270 - V_{CB} + 1 \times I_C = 0\] \[V_{CB} = 2.5 - 270 \times 0.025 = -4.25\,\text{V}\] From above figure, collector to base junction is in reverse bias. Therefore, the transistor is in forward active region. Hence, the correct option is (D).
Method 2
Assuming transistor is in saturation region, \[V_{EB(\text{sat})} = 0.8\,\text{V}, \quad V_{EC(\text{sat})} = 0.2\,\text{V}\] For transistor to be in saturation region, \[I_{B(\text{min})} \le I_B \implies \frac{I_{C(\text{sat})}}{\beta} \le I_B \quad \dots \text{(i)}\] Applying KVL in loop (1), \[-10 + 1 \times (I_B + I_{C(\text{sat})}) + V_{EB(\text{sat})} = 0\] \[271 I_B + I_{C(\text{sat})} = 9.3 \quad \dots \text{(ii)}\] Applying KVL in loop (3), \[-10 + 1 \times (I_B + I_{C(\text{sat})}) + V_{EC(\text{sat})} + 1 \times I_{C(\text{sat})} = 0\] \[I_B + 2 I_{C(\text{sat})} = 9.8 \quad \dots \text{(iii)}\] From equation (ii) and (iii), \[I_B = 0.016\,\text{mA}\] \[I_{C(\text{sat})} = 4.89\,\text{mA}\] From equation (i), \[I_{B(\text{min})} = \frac{I_{C(\text{sat})}}{\beta} = \frac{4.89}{100} = 0.048\,\text{mA}\] Hence, \(I_{B(\text{min})} > I_B \quad \dots \text{(iv)}\) From equation (i) and (iv), the transistor does not satisfy the condition of saturation. Hence, our assumption is wrong. Therefore, the transistor is in forward active region.
\[\boxed{\text{(D) Forward active region}}\]
Key points
  • For a \(p\)-\(n\)-\(p\) transistor, forward active region requires \(V_{EB} > 0\) (emitter-base junction forward biased) and \(V_{CB} < 0\) (collector-base junction reverse biased).
  • If saturation mode analysis yields \(I_B < I_{B(\text{min})}\), the transistor operates in the active region.

questions.question: A, B, C and D are input bits and \(Y\) is the output bit in the XOR gate circuit shown below. Which of the following statements about the sum \(S\) of \(A\), \(B\), \(C\), \(D\) and \(Y\) is correct?

questions.explanation:
Given: HEX number \((AB.CD)_{16}\) Integer part → Octal:
To convert the integer part of the binary number into octal, form groups of three bits starting from the LSB: \[\underbrace{010}_{2}\;\underbrace{101}_{5}\;\underbrace{011}_{3} \qquad \Rightarrow \quad \text{Integer part (octal)} = 253\] (A leading 0 is added to complete the leftmost group of 3.) Fractional part → Octal:

Method 1
Block Diagram Reduction: img/ch2_block_diagram_and_signal_flow_graph/2_07_1_A.png The target reduced block diagram has the overall transfer function: \[\frac{C}{R} = \frac{X Y P}{1 - Y P Z}\] From the above block diagram : \[C = P X_4 \implies X_4 = \frac{C}{P}\] \[X_1 = R c_0 + C b_0 - X_4 a_0 \implies X_1 = R c_0 + C b_0 - \frac{C a_0}{P}\] \[X_2 = \frac{X_1}{s} = \frac{R c_0}{s} + \frac{C b_0}{s} - \frac{C a_0}{P s}\] \[X_3 = X_2 - X_4 a_1 + C b_1 + R c_1\] \[X_3 = \frac{R c_0}{s} + \frac{C b_0}{s} - \frac{C a_0}{P s} - \frac{C a_1}{P} + C b_1 + R c_1\] \[X_4 = \frac{X_3}{s}\] \[\frac{C}{P} = \frac{R c_0}{s^2} + \frac{C b_0}{s^2} - \frac{C a_0}{P s^2} - \frac{C a_1}{P s} + \frac{C b_1}{s} + \frac{R c_1}{s}\] Rearranging terms to separate \(C\) and \(R\): \[\frac{C}{R} = \frac{P [c_1 s + c_0]}{s^2 + a_1 s + a_0 - P [b_1 s + b_0]}\] \[\frac{C}{R} = \frac{\dfrac{P [c_1 s + c_0]}{s^2 + a_1 s + a_0}}{1 - \dfrac{P [b_1 s + b_0]}{s^2 + a_1 s + a_0}}\] Comparing this with the target format \(\frac{X Y P}{1 - Y P Z}\): \[X = c_1 s + c_0 \quad Y = \frac{1}{s^2 + a_1 s + a_0} \quad Z = b_1 s + b_0\]
Method 2
Signal Flow Graph (SFG) Method: img/ch2_block_diagram_and_signal_flow_graph/2_07_1_B.png Using Mason's Gain Formula, the forward path gains are: \[P_1 = \frac{P c_0}{s^2}, \quad P_2 = \frac{P c_1}{s}\] The individual feedback loop gains are: \[L_1 = -\frac{a_1}{s}, \quad L_2 = -\frac{a_0}{s^2} \quad L_3 = \frac{P b_0}{s^2}, \quad L_4 = \frac{P b_1}{s}\] The system determinant (\(\Delta\)) with no non-touching loops: \[\Delta = 1 - (L_1 + L_2 + L_3 + L_4)\] \[\Delta = 1 - \left( -\frac{a_1}{s} - \frac{a_0}{s^2} + \frac{P b_0}{s^2} + \frac{P b_1}{s} \right)\] Since all loops touch both forward paths, \(\Delta_1 = 1\) and \(\Delta_2 = 1\). The overall transfer function is: \[\frac{C}{R} = \frac{P_1 \Delta_1 + P_2 \Delta_2}{\Delta}\] \[\frac{C}{R}= \frac{\dfrac{P c_0}{s^2} + \dfrac{P c_1}{s}}{1 + \dfrac{a_1}{s} + \dfrac{a_0}{s^2} - \dfrac{P b_1}{s} - \dfrac{P b_0}{s^2}}\] \[\frac{C}{R} = \frac{P(c_1 s + c_0)}{s^2 + a_1 s + a_0 - P(b_1 s + b_0)}\] \[\frac{C}{R} = \frac{(c_1 s + c_0) \cdot \left(\dfrac{1}{s^2 + a_1 s + a_0}\right) \cdot P}{1 - \left(\dfrac{1}{s^2 + a_1 s + a_0}\right) \cdot P \cdot (b_1 s + b_0)}\] Comparing with \(\frac{X Y P}{1 - Y P Z}\), we directly obtain: \[X = c_1 s + c_0, \quad Y = \frac{1}{s^2 + a_1 s + a_0}, \quad Z = b_1 s + b_0\]

questions.question: Consider the feedback control system shown below which is subjected to a unit step input. The system is stable and has the following parameters \(k_p = 4\), \(k_i = 10\), \(\omega = 500\) and \(\xi = 0.7\). The steady state value of \(z\) is
questions.explanation: From the given block diagram, the error signal is: \[E(s) = R(s) - C(s)\] The relationship for the variable \(Z(s)\) is: \[Z(s) = \left(\frac{k_i}{s}\right) E(s)\] The overall open-loop transfer function \(G(s)\) is: \[G(s) = \left(k_p + \frac{k_i}{s}\right)\left(\frac{\omega^2}{s^2 + 2\xi\omega s + \omega^2}\right)\] Since \(H(s) = 1\), the closed-loop expression for \(E(s)\) is: \[E(s) = \frac{R(s)}{1 + G(s)H(s)} = \frac{R(s)}{1 + G(s)}\] Substituting \(E(s)\) into the expression for \(Z(s)\): \[Z(s) = \frac{k_i}{s} \cdot \frac{R(s)}{1 + G(s)}\] Given a unit step input, \(R(s) = \frac{1}{s}\). Thus: \[Z(s) = \frac{k_i}{s^2[1 + G(s)]}\] Applying the Final Value Theorem to find the steady-state value \(z_{ss}\): \[z_{ss} = \lim_{s \to 0} s Z(s) = \lim_{s \to 0} \frac{s \cdot \dfrac{k_i}{s} \cdot \dfrac{1}{s}}{1 + \left(k_p + \dfrac{k_i}{s}\right)\left(\dfrac{\omega^2}{s^2 + 2\xi\omega s + \omega^2}\right)}\] Multiplying the numerator and denominator by \(s\): \[z_{ss} = \lim_{s \to 0} \frac{k_i}{s + (s k_p + k_i)\left(\dfrac{\omega^2}{s^2 + 2\xi\omega s + \omega^2}\right)}\] \[z_{ss} = \frac{k_i}{0 + (0 + k_i)\left(\dfrac{\omega^2}{0 + 0 + \omega^2}\right)} = \frac{k_i}{k_i (1)} = 1\] \[\boxed{(A) \ \ 1}\]

Common data for Q3.07.2 and Q3.07.3 Consider the R-L-C circuit shown in figure.

For a step-input \(e_i\), the overshoot in the output \(e_o\) will be
options: 0, since the system is not under-damping
questions.explanation:
Given a series \(R-L-C\) circuit with parameters: \(R = 10\,\Omega\), \(L = 1\,\text{mH}\), and \(C = 10\,\mu\text{F}\). The loop equation for the circuit is: \[e_i = R i + L \frac{di}{dt} + \frac{1}{C} \int i \, dt\] Taking the Laplace transform on both sides (assuming zero initial conditions): \[E_i(s) = \left( R + Ls + \frac{1}{Cs} \right) I(s) \implies I(s) = \frac{E_i(s)}{R + Ls + \frac{1}{Cs}}\] The output voltage \(e_o\) across the capacitor is given by: \[e_o = \frac{1}{C} \int i \, dt\] \[E_o(s) = \frac{1}{Cs} I(s) = \frac{1}{Cs} \left[ \frac{E_i(s)}{R + Ls + \frac{1}{Cs}} \right]\] The transfer function of the system is: \[\frac{E_o(s)}{E_i(s)} = \frac{1}{LC \left( s^2 + \frac{R}{L}s + \frac{1}{LC} \right)}\] The characteristic equation is obtained by setting the denominator to zero: \[s^2 + \frac{R}{L}s + \frac{1}{LC} = 0\] Comparing this with the standard second-order characteristic equation \(s^2 + 2\xi\omega_n s + \omega_n^2 = 0\): \[\omega_n = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}, \quad \xi = \frac{R}{2L\omega_n} = \frac{R}{2}\sqrt{\frac{C}{L}}\] \[\xi = \frac{10}{2} \sqrt{\frac{10 \times 10^{-6}}{1 \times 10^{-3}}} = 5 \times \sqrt{10^{-2}} = 0.5\] Since \(\xi = 0.5\) (where \(0 < \xi < 1\)), the system is under-damped. The peak overshoot (\(M_p\)) for a step input is given by: \[M_p= e^{-\pi\xi / \sqrt{1-\xi^2}}= e^{-\pi \times 0.5 / \sqrt{1-0.5^2}} = e^{-1.8138} \approx 0.163 \text{ or } 16.3\%\] \[\boxed{(C) \ \ 16\%}\]
Key points
For a standard second-order system, the damping ratio for a series \(R-L-C\) circuit is given by \(\xi = \frac{R}{2}\sqrt{\frac{C}{L}}\).
Mistakes to avoid
Radian vs Degree Mode: When computing the exponent value \(\frac{\pi\xi}{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}\), ensure your calculator handles \(\pi\) as a mathematical constant (\(\approx 3.14159\)) rather than treating trigonometric expressions in degree mode incorrectly.

If the above step response is to be observed on a non-storage CRO, then it would be best to have the \(e_i\) as a
questions.explanation:
From the characteristic parameters of the given series \(R-L-C\) network layout: \[\omega_n = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 \times 10^{-3} \times 10 \times 10^{-6}}} = 10^4\,\text{rad/s}\] Given that the damping ratio \(\xi = 0.5\), the settling time (\(t_s\)) for a \(2\%\) tolerance band is: \[t_s = \frac{4}{\xi\omega_n} = \frac{4}{0.5 \times 10^4} = 0.8\,\text{ms}\] To view a transient step response cleanly on a non-storage Cathode Ray Oscilloscope (CRO), a single step function is unsuitable because the trace fades away immediately. Instead, a periodic square wave input is applied to repeatedly trigger the response. For an optimal visual presentation of the entire transient period up to stabilization, the duration of each half-cycle (\(\frac{T}{2}\)) must be strictly greater than the settling time (\(t_s\)), but not excessively large: \[\frac{T}{2} > t_s \implies \frac{1}{2f} > 0.8\,\text{ms}\] Let us evaluate the available frequency choices:
  • For \(f = 50\,\text{Hz}\):
    \[\frac{T}{2} = \frac{1}{2 \times 50} = 10\,\text{ms} \gg 0.8\,\text{ms}\] Since \(10\,\text{ms}\) is much larger than \(0.8\,\text{ms}\), the transient phase finishes within a tiny fraction (\(8\%\)) of the display time, leaving the remaining \(9.2\,\text{ms}\) as a flat line.
  • For \(f = 300\,\text{Hz}\):
    \[\frac{T}{2} = \frac{1}{2 \times 300} \approx 1.67\,\text{ms} > 0.8\,\text{ms}\] The transient is completely visible and takes up a balanced portion of the sweep screen profile.
  • For \(f = 2.0\,\text{kHz}\):
    \[\frac{T}{2} = \frac{1}{2 \times 2 \times 10^3} = 0.25\,\text{ms} < 0.8\,\text{ms}\] The square wave switches before the transient settles down completely.
Therefore, a square wave of \(50\,\text{Hz}\) or \(300\,\text{Hz}\) allows complete settlement, but \(300\,\text{Hz}\) provides the best representation of the transient details without a long flat line. \[\boxed{\text{(C) square wave of frequency 300 Hz}}\]
Key points
  • Non-storage CROs need periodic signals like square waves to persistently display transient behaviors via repeated sweeps.
  • The half-period interval constraint criteria requires \(\frac{T}{2} \ge t_s\) to avoid truncation of transient information.

questions.question: The system shown in the figure is
options: stable for input \(u_1\), but unstable for input \(u_2\)
questions.explanation:
To determine the stability of the multi-input multi-output (MIMO) system, we analyze its stability under individual inputs using the superposition principle. Case 1: Considering input \(u_1(s)\) alone :
The block diagram reduces to a standard negative feedback loop configuration: img/ch4_rouths_stability_criterion/4_07_1_A.jpg The corresponding closed-loop transfer function is given by: \[TF_1 = \frac{Y_1(s)}{U_1(s)} = \frac{\dfrac{s-1}{s+2}}{1 + \left(\dfrac{s-1}{s+2}\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{s-1}\right)}\] \[TF_1 = \frac{\dfrac{s-1}{s+2}}{1 + \dfrac{1}{s+2}} = \frac{s-1}{s+3}\] The pole is located at \(s = -3\), which lies entirely on the left-hand side (LHS) of the \(s\)-plane. Hence, the system is stable with respect to input \(u_1\). Case 2: Considering input \(u_2(s)\) alone :
The block diagram reduces to a standard negative feedback loop configuration: img/ch4_rouths_stability_criterion/4_07_1_B.jpg The corresponding closed-loop transfer function is given by: \[TF_2 = \frac{Y_2(s)}{U_2(s)} = \frac{\dfrac{1}{s-1}}{1 + \left(\dfrac{1}{s-1}\right)\left(\dfrac{s-1}{s+2}\right)}\] \[TF_2 = \frac{\dfrac{1}{s-1}}{\dfrac{(s+2) + 1}{s+2}} = \frac{s+2}{(s-1)(s+3)}\] The system has poles at \(s = -3\) and \(s = 1\). The pole at \(s = 1\) lies on the right-hand side (RHS) of the \(s\)-plane. Hence, the system is unstable with respect to input \(u_2\). \[\boxed{\text{(D) stable for input $u_1$, but unstable for input $u_2$}}\]
Key points
MIMO Stability Criterion: For a multi-input system to be stable, the transfer functions corresponding to every single input channel must be stable (all poles must reside strictly in the LHS of the \(s\)-plane).

In a transformer, zero voltage regulation at full load is
options: possible at unity power factor load
possible at leading power factor load
possible at lagging power factor load
questions.explanation:
The voltage regulation versus power factor angle curve for a transformer is shown below. [figure unavailable] For a transformer, approximate voltage regulation is \[\%VR = \frac{I_2R_{eq}\cos\phi \pm I_2X_{eq}\sin\phi}{V_2} \times100\] For lagging power factor, \[\%VR = \frac{I_2R_{eq}\cos\phi + I_2X_{eq}\sin\phi}{V_2} \times100\] For leading power factor, \[\%VR = \frac{I_2R_{eq}\cos\phi - I_2X_{eq}\sin\phi}{V_2} \times100\] Zero voltage regulation is possible when \[I_2R_{eq}\cos\phi = I_2X_{eq}\sin\phi\] This condition occurs only at leading power factor of load. Hence, right option is \[\boxed{\text{C}}\]
Key points
  • Voltage regulation can be positive, zero, or negative depending on load power factor.
  • Lagging power factor generally gives positive voltage regulation.
  • Leading power factor can give zero or negative voltage regulation.

Statement for Linked Questions Q3.08.1 and Q3.08.2:
A \(240\,\text{V}\), dc shunt motor draws \(15\,\text{A}\) while supplying the rated load at a speed of \(80\,\text{rad/s}\). The armature resistance is \(0.5\,\Omega\) and the field winding resistance is \(80\,\Omega\).

The dc motor, which can provide zero speed regulation at full load without any controller, is
questions.explanation:
For zero speed regulation, the motor speed must remain constant from no-load to full-load. For a DC motor, \[N \propto \frac{E_b}{\phi}\] \[E_b = V - I_aR_a\] At full-load, \(I_a\) increases, so the armature voltage drop \(I_aR_a\) increases and \(E_b\) decreases. For speed to remain constant, the flux \(\phi\) must also decrease in the same proportion. This condition is achieved in a differential compound motor, because the series field opposes the shunt field. Hence, as load increases, the net flux decreases and compensates for the fall in back emf. \[\boxed{D}\]
Key points
  • Zero speed regulation means no change in speed from no-load to full-load.
  • In a differential compound motor, net flux decreases with increase in load.
  • Decrease in flux compensates the decrease in back emf, keeping speed nearly constant.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not choose DC shunt motor; it gives good but not zero speed regulation.
  • Do not choose DC series motor; it has very poor speed regulation.
  • Remember that differential compounding reduces flux with load.

The electromagnetic torque \(T_e\) of a drive and its connected load torque \(T_L\) are as shown below. Out of the operating points A, B, C and D, the stable ones are [figure unavailable] [figure unavailable]
questions.explanation:
For stability of an induction motor operating point, \[\frac{dT_{e}}{dn}<\frac{dT_{L}}{dn}\] where \(T_{e}\) is the electromagnetic torque and \(T_{L}\) is the load torque. At point A, \[\frac{dT_{e}}{dn}<0,
\qquad
\frac{dT_{L}}{dn}>0\] Hence, \[\frac{dT_{e}}{dn}<\frac{dT_{L}}{dn}\] So, A is a stable operating point. At point B, \[\frac{dT_{e}}{dn}>\frac{dT_{L}}{dn}\] So, B is an unstable operating point. At point C, \[\frac{dT_{e}}{dn}<\frac{dT_{L}}{dn}\] So, C is a stable operating point. At point D, both slopes are negative, but \[\frac{dT_{e}}{dn}\] is more negative as compared to \[\frac{dT_{L}}{dn}\] Therefore, \[\frac{dT_{L}}{dn}>\frac{dT_{e}}{dn}\] Hence, D is also a stable operating point. Therefore, the stable operating points are A, C and D. \[\boxed{A}\]

questions.question: A three-phase, three-stack, variable reluctance step motor has \(20\) poles on each rotor and stator stack. The step angle of this step motor is
questions.explanation:
For a multi-stack variable reluctance stepper motor, the step angle is given by \[\beta=\frac{360^\circ}{mP_r}\] where
  • \(m\) = number of stacks
  • \(P_r\) = number of rotor poles
Given, \[m=3,\qquad P_r=20\] Substituting, \[\beta=\frac{360^\circ}{3\times20}\] \[\beta=6^\circ\] Therefore, the correct option is \[\boxed{\text{ B}}\]
Key points
  • For a multi-stack variable reluctance stepper motor, the step angle is given by \(\beta=\dfrac{360^\circ}{mP_r}\).
  • The step angle decreases as the number of stacks or rotor poles increases.
  • Smaller step angle provides higher positioning resolution.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not use the permanent-magnet/hybrid stepper motor formula \(\beta=\dfrac{(P_s-P_r)}{P_sP_r}\times360^\circ\) for a multi-stack variable reluctance motor.
  • Do not confuse the number of stacks with the number of phases.
  • Ensure rotor poles per stack are used in the calculation.

The transient reactance \(x'\) of the generator is \(0.1\) pu and the mechanical power input to it is constant at \(1.0\) pu. Due to some previous disturbance, the rotor angle \((\delta)\) is undergoing an undamped oscillation, with the maximum value of \(\delta(t)\) equal to \(130^\circ\). One of the parallel lines trips due to relay maloperation at an instant when \(\delta(t)=130^\circ\) as shown in the figure. The maximum value of the per unit line reactance, \(x\), such that the system does not lose synchronism subsequent to this tripping is
questions.explanation: At the instant of relay maloperation, the rotor angle is already at its maximum value, \[\delta_{\max}=130^\circ\] Since the mechanical input power remains constant at \[P_m = 1.0\ \text{pu}\] the system will remain stable only if the post-disturbance electrical power is capable of balancing the mechanical input at \(\delta = 130^\circ\). After one transmission line trips, the equivalent transfer reactance becomes \[X_{eq}=x' + x = 0.1 + x\] For a generator connected to an infinite bus, \[P_e=\frac{EV}{X_{eq}}\sin\delta\] Taking \(E=V=1\) pu, \[1=\frac{1}{0.1+x}\sin130^\circ\] \[0.1+x=\sin130^\circ\] \[0.1+x=0.766\] \[x=0.666\] \[x \approx 0.67\ \text{pu}\] \[\boxed{\text{(C)} \ 0.67}\]

Consider the two power systems shown in figure A below, which are initially not interconnected, and are operating in steady state at the same frequency. Separate loadflow solutions are computed individually for the two systems, corresponding to this scenario. The bus voltage phasors so obtained are indicated on figure A. These two isolated systems are now interconnected by a short transmission line as shown in figure B, and it is found that \(P_1=P_2=Q_1=Q_2=0\). The bus voltage phase angular difference between generator bus X and generator bus Y after the interconnection is
questions.explanation:
Since \[P_1=P_2=Q_1=Q_2=0,\] there is no real or reactive power transfer through the interconnecting transmission line. For a short transmission line carrying zero complex power, the voltages at both ends must be identical in magnitude and phase. Let the common bus voltage after interconnection be \[V = 1.02\angle 0^\circ.\] System X
Before interconnection, the generator voltages are \[1.02\angle 0^\circ \quad \text{and} \quad 1.02\angle 10^\circ\] while bus X is \[V_X = 1.0\angle 20^\circ.\] To make the interconnection bus voltage equal to \[1.02\angle 0^\circ,\] all voltages in the left system shift by \[+30^\circ.\] Hence, \[V_X = 1.0\angle (20^\circ+10^\circ) = 1.0\angle 30^\circ.\] System Y
Before interconnection, the generator voltages are \[1.02\angle 0^\circ \quad \text{and} \quad 1.02\angle 15^\circ\] while bus Y is \[V_Y = 1.0\angle (-5^\circ).\] To make the interconnection bus voltage equal to \[1.02\angle 0^\circ,\] all voltages in the right system shift by \[+25^\circ.\] Therefore, \[V_Y = 1.0\angle (-5^\circ+25^\circ) = 1.0\angle 20^\circ.\] Hence, the phase angular difference between buses X and Y is \[\angle X-\angle Y = 30^\circ-20^\circ = 10^\circ.\] Hence, the correct answer is \[\boxed{\text{(A)} \ 10^\circ}\]

The figure below shows a three phase self-commutated voltage source converter connected to a power system. The converter's dc bus capacitor is marked as C in the figure. The circuit is initially operating in steady state with \(\delta=0\) and the capacitor dc voltage is equal to \(V_{dc0}\). You may neglect all losses and harmonics. What action should be taken to increase the capacitor dc voltage slowly to a new steady state value?
options: Make \(\delta\) positive and maintain it at a positive value
Make \(\delta\) positive and return it to its original value
Make \(\delta\) negative and maintain it at a negative value
Make \(\delta\) negative and return it to its original value
questions.explanation:
Initially, \[\delta = 0\] and the converter dc capacitor voltage is \[V_C = V_{dc0}.\] Since losses are neglected, any increase in the capacitor energy must come from real power supplied by the AC system. The real power exchanged between two voltage sources connected through a reactance is \[P=\frac{EV}{X}\sin\delta.\] At \[\delta=0,\] \[P=0.\] To increase the capacitor dc voltage, energy must flow from the AC system into the converter. Therefore the converter voltage phasor must lag the system voltage phasor so that real power flows from the AC system to the converter. This is achieved by making \[\delta < 0.\] The incoming real power charges the dc capacitor and increases its stored energy. Once the desired dc voltage is reached, the power transfer must again become zero to maintain the new steady-state voltage. Therefore, \[\delta\] must be returned to its original value \[\delta = 0.\] Hence, the required action is: \[\boxed{\text{(D) Make }\delta\text{ negative and return it to its original value}}\]
Key points
  • The dc capacitor voltage increases only when net real power enters the converter.
  • Real power transfer through a reactance is governed by: \[P=\frac{EV}{X}\sin\delta.\]
  • A negative converter angle causes power to flow from the AC system into the converter.
  • After the capacitor reaches the desired voltage, \(\delta\) must return to zero so that charging ceases.

questions.question: Consider a bundled conductor of an overhead transmission line consisting of three identical sub-conductors placed at the corners of an equilateral triangle as shown in the figure. Neglect the charges on the other phase conductors and ground. Assume that the spacing between sub-conductors is much larger than their radius. The maximum electric field intensity is experienced at
questions.explanation:
Each sub-conductor produces its own radial electric field at its surface, while the remaining two sub-conductors produce additional electric fields whose magnitudes depend on the bundle spacing. Since the conductor radius is much smaller than the spacing between adjacent sub-conductors, \[r\ll d,\] The electric field due to the conductor on whose surface the observation point lies is much larger than the fields contributed by the other two conductors. Hence, instead of assuming equal magnitudes, only the directions of the individual field vectors are used to compare the resultant electric field at different points. At Point \(Y\)
Point \(Y\) lies on the outer surface of the upper conductor. The electric field due to the upper conductor is directed radially outward. The fields produced by the other two sub-conductors also have outward components at this location. Consequently, these components add constructively, producing the largest resultant electric field. At Point \(X\)
Point \(X\) lies on the inner surface of the upper conductor. Although the upper conductor still produces a radial outward field, the fields due to the other two sub-conductors are directed towards the bundle centre and therefore oppose the conductor's own field. As a result, the resultant electric field is reduced. At Point \(Z\)
At Point \(Z\), the field contributions from the adjacent sub-conductors partially cancel each other due to symmetry. The resultant electric field is therefore intermediate between those at Points \(Y\) and \(X\). At Point \(W\)
At Point \(W\), the contributions from the neighbouring conductors oppose one another most effectively because of symmetry, giving the minimum resultant electric field among the four points. Hence, \[E_Y>E_Z>E_X>E_W.\] Therefore, the maximum electric field intensity occurs at the outermost point of the bundle, \[\boxed{\text{Point Y}}\] Hence, the correct answer is \[\boxed{\text{(B) Point Y}}\]

questions.question: Consider the protection system shown in the figure below. The circuit breakers numbered from 1 to 7 are of identical type. A single line-to-ground fault with zero fault impedance occurs at the midpoint of the line (at point F), but circuit breaker 4 fails to operate (stuck breaker). If the relays are coordinated correctly, a valid sequence of circuit-breaker operation is
questions.explanation:
A single line-to-ground fault occurs at the midpoint of the transmission line connected between buses B and C. The fault lies within the protection zone bounded by circuit breakers \[4,\;5,\;6,\;7\] Under normal operation, the primary protection should isolate the fault by tripping the breakers nearest to the faulted section. Since circuit breaker \(4\) is stuck and fails to open, the fault remains energized from the left side. Step 1: Primary protection operation
The healthy end of the faulted line is disconnected first. Therefore, \[\boxed{5}\] operates first. Step 2: Breaker-failure backup protection
Breaker \(4\) fails to clear the fault. Breaker-failure protection associated with breaker \(4\) initiates tripping of all breakers connected to the same bus section to completely de-energize the fault contribution feeding through breaker \(4\). Hence the associated breakers operate in sequence as \[6 \rightarrow 7 \rightarrow 3\] thereby isolating the bus section connected to the failed breaker. Step 3: Remote backup protection
If fault current still persists, remote backup protection on the adjacent transmission line operates. Consequently, \[1 \rightarrow 2\] trip subsequently. Thus a valid coordinated sequence is \[5,\;6,\;7,\;3,\;1,\;2\] Hence, the correct answer is \[\boxed{\text{(C) Sequence } = 5,6,7,3,1,2}\]
Key points
  • Primary protection must operate before backup protection.
  • Breaker-failure (stuck-breaker) protection is activated when a breaker receives a trip command but fails to interrupt current.
  • Backup protection isolates all possible sources feeding the fault.
  • Remote backup relays operate with intentional time delay after local backup protection.

The resistance \(R\) should be
questions.explanation:
[figure unavailable] When the transistor is ON, its collector-emitter voltage drop is \(1\,\text{V}\). Hence, the voltage across the primary winding is \[V_1=10-1=9\,\text{V}.\] Since the pulse transformer has a turns ratio of \(1:1\), \[V_2=V_1=9\,\text{V}.\] During the pulse, \(D_1\) is forward biased and drops \(1\,\text{V}\), and the SCR gate-cathode junction also drops \(1\,\text{V}\).   • Pulse transformer secondary voltage equals primary voltage for a \(1:1\) transformer.
  • Gate resistor is selected from allowable gate current.

A single phase full-wave half-controlled bridge converter feeds an inductive load. The two SCRs in the converter are connected to a common DC bus. The converter has to have a freewheeling diode.
options: because the converter inherently does not provide for free-wheeling.
because the converter does not provide for free-wheeling for high values of triggering angles.
or else the free-wheeling action of the converter will cause shorting of the AC supply.
or else if a gate pulse to one of the SCRs is missed, it will subsequently cause a high load current in the other SCR.
questions.explanation:
A free-wheeling diode is required to prevent short-circuiting, which can occur if the current from one set of thyristors is not completely transferred before the other set of thyristors starts conducting. \[\boxed{C}\]
Key points
  • A free-wheeling diode provides an alternate path for the load current during commutation.
  • It prevents simultaneous conduction of two thyristor groups, thereby avoiding source short-circuit.
  • It improves commutation reliability and reduces voltage spikes across the thyristors.

A three-phase, \(440\,\text{V}\), \(50\,\text{Hz}\) ac mains fed thyristor bridge is feeding a \(440\,\text{V}\) dc, \(15\,\text{kW}\), \(1500\,\text{rpm}\) separately excited dc motor with a ripple free continuous current in dc link under all operating conditions. Neglecting the losses, the power factor of the ac mains at half the rated speed, is
questions.explanation:
Back emf of the motor is \[E_a=V_o-I_aR_a\] Here, \(V_o\) is the average output voltage of the converter. Since losses are neglected, \[R_a=0\] Therefore, \[E_a=V_o\] Also, \[V_o=E_a=K\phi N\] At \(440\,\text{V}\) dc voltage, speed is \(1500\,\text{rpm}\). At half the rated speed, \[N=750\,\text{rpm}\] Hence, \[V_o=220\,\text{V}\] If \(I_a\) is the average armature current, then rms value of supply current is \[I_s=I_a\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\] Power delivered to the motor is \[P=V_oI_a\] Input volt-ampere is \[\text{Input VA}=\sqrt{3}V_sI_s\] Therefore, input power factor is \[\text{Input power factor} = \frac{V_oI_a}{\sqrt{3}V_sI_s}\] \[= \frac{220I_a}{\sqrt{3}\times440\times I_a\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}}\] \[=0.354\] \[\boxed{A}\]
Key points
  • With \(R_a=0\), motor back emf is equal to the converter average output voltage.
  • For constant flux, \[E_a\propto N.\]
  • For this converter, \[I_s=I_a\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}.\]
  • Input power factor is \[\text{IPF}=\frac{\text{Output power}}{\text{Input VA}}.\]

A single-phase, \(230\,\text{V}\), \(50\,\text{Hz}\) ac mains fed step down transformer \((4\!:\!1)\) is supplying power to a half-wave uncontrolled ac-dc converter used for charging a battery \((12\,\text{V dc})\) with the series current limiting resistor being \(19.04\,\Omega\). The charging current is
questions.explanation:
The input to the converter is \[V_s=\frac{230}{4}=57.5\,\text{V}\] The diode conducts when \[V_s\geq E.\] Hence, the diode starts conducting at \(\theta_1\) such that \[V_m\sin\theta_1=E\] \[57.5\sqrt{2}\sin\theta_1=12\] \[\theta_1=8.486^\circ=0.148\,\text{rad}\] The average output current is \[I_o=\frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{\theta_1}^{\pi-\theta_1} \left(\frac{V_m\sin\omega t-E}{R}\right) d(\omega t)\] \[I_o = \frac{1}{2\pi R} \left[ 2V_m\cos\theta_1 - E(\pi-2\theta_1) \right]\] \[= \frac{1}{2\pi\times19.04} \left[ 2\times57.5\sqrt{2}\times\cos8.486^\circ - 12\left(\pi-2\times0.148\right) \right]\] \[I_o=1.06\,\text{A}\approx1\,\text{A}\] \[\boxed{D}\]
Key points
  • Diode conduction starts when the instantaneous source voltage equals the opposing emf.
  • Conduction angle is from \(\theta_1\) to \(\pi-\theta_1\).
  • The average output current is obtained by integrating the load current over the conduction interval.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not assume conduction starts at \(0^\circ\); it starts when \(V_m\sin\theta_1=E\).
  • Use \(\theta_1\) in radians while evaluating the integral term \((\pi-2\theta_1)\).
  • Do not forget to divide the integral by \(2\pi\) to obtain the average current.

``Six MOSFETs connected in a bridge configuration (having no other power device) MUST be operated as a Voltage Source Inverter (VSI).'' This statement is:
options: True, because being majority carrier devices, MOSFETs are voltage driven.
True, because MOSFETs have inherently anti-parallel diodes.
False, because it can be operated both as a Current Source Inverter (CSI) and as a Voltage Source Inverter (VSI).
False, because MOSFETs can be operated as excellent constant current sources in the saturation region.
questions.explanation: A Voltage Source Inverter (VSI) requires each switch to conduct current in both directions while blocking reverse voltage. A power MOSFET has an inherent anti-parallel body diode, which provides the necessary reverse current path required in a VSI. However, because of this body diode, a MOSFET cannot block reverse voltage and hence cannot be directly used in a Current Source Inverter (CSI). Therefore, six MOSFETs connected in a bridge configuration (without any additional power devices) must be operated as a Voltage Source Inverter (VSI). Hence, the correct answer is \[\boxed{(B)\ \text{True, because MOSFETs have inherently anti-parallel diodes}}\]

questions.question: A bridge circuit is shown in the figure below. Which one of the sequence given below is most suitable for balancing the bridge? [figure unavailable]
questions.explanation: [figure unavailable] The bridge arms are: \[Z_1=R_1+jX_1,\qquad Z_2=R_2,\qquad Z_3=R_3,\qquad Z_4=R_4-jX_4\] At balance, \[Z_1Z_4=Z_2Z_3\] So, \[(R_1+jX_1)(R_4-jX_4)=R_2R_3\] Expanding, \[R_1R_4+X_1X_4+j(X_1R_4-R_1X_4)=R_2R_3\] Equating real and imaginary parts, \[R_1R_4+X_1X_4=R_2R_3,\qquad X_1R_4=R_1X_4\] The imaginary equation must be satisfied first, so the phase balance is set by adjusting \(R_4\). After that, \(R_1\) is adjusted to obtain final balance. The solution where any one or both of \(R_1\) or \(R_4\) is/are 0 is also possible as the branch will not get shorted due to inductor and capacitor. Hence, the correct sequence is: \[\boxed{\text{First adjust }R_4,\text{ then adjust }R_1}\] Why others are wrong B. First adjust \(R_2\), then adjust \(R_3\) \(\times\) Both appear only in the real-balance term \(R_2R_3\). They cannot satisfy \[X_1R_4=R_1X_4\] so phase balance is ignored. C. First adjust \(R_2\), then adjust \(R_4\) \(\times\) The branch resistance \(R_2\) should not be zero while satisfying the real part equation/ D. First adjust \(R_4\), then adjust \(R_2\) \(\times\) The first step is correct, but the second step the branch resistance \(R_2\) should not be zero while satisfying the real part equation. Therefore, the correct option is \[\boxed{\textbf{A. } \text{First adjust} \ R_4,\text{ then adjust}\ R1}\]

Then the ``signal'' and ``ground'' probes \(S_1\), \(G_1\) and \(S_2\), \(G_2\) of \(\text{Ch}_1\) and \(\text{Ch}_2\), respectively, are connected to points [figure unavailable]
questions.explanation: [figure unavailable] The circuit is a series \(RL\) circuit driven by a square wave input. A non-isolated CRO has both channel grounds internally connected, so: \[G_1\equiv G_2\] Hence both ground clips must be connected to the same circuit point. From the given waveforms, the common reference point is \(B\). Therefore, \[G_1=G_2=B\] Now, channel 1 waveform starts from zero and rises exponentially, which is the voltage across the resistor in an \(RL\) transient. Hence the signal probe for Ch1 must be at \(A\), so that \[V_{AB}=V_R\] Channel 2 waveform starts from high (in negative) and decays exponentially to zero, which is the voltage across the inductor. The ground is already at \(B\), is the reason for getting negative value. The signal probe for Ch2 must be at \(C\), so that \[V_{BC}=V_L\] Therefore the correct connection is: \[\boxed{\textbf{B. }A,\ B,\ C,\ B}\]
